data.text:
I ran one search per claim. Claims 0 and 3 are only partly supported as written.

**Claim 0: Silicon is made by heating quartz sand with carbon in an arc furnace at roughly 1,900 to 2,000 °C.**
**Verdict: supported in a corrected form.** The process is right, but the sources give a wider temperature range for industrial furnaces.
- Elkem, a silicon producer, describes mixing quartz with carbon material (coal, coke, charcoal, woodchips) and heating it to "about 1500–2000 °C in a submerged electric arc furnace." (https://magazine.elkem.com/material-science-insights/from-quartz-to-silicon-to-silicones/)
- A South African journal paper says silica is reduced by carbon in a submerged arc furnace "at temperatures between 1300 and 2000°C under atmospheric pressure." The charge is quartz, sand or quartzite, plus coke, coal, charcoal and wood chips. (https://www.scielo.org.za/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S2225-62532018000200011, also https://www.saimm.co.za/Journal/v118n02p143.pdf)
- The 1900–2000 °C figure appears in a research paper on a small electric arc furnace that recycled silicon from solar-wafer cutting waste. It is not a general industrial figure. (https://www.researchgate.net/publication/331835055_Recycling_high_purity_silicon_from_solar_grade_silicon_cutting_slurry_waste_by_carbothermic_reduction_in_the_electric_arc_furnace)
- Corrected line: "heated with carbon in an electric arc furnace at up to about 2,000 °C." Industry ranges run from roughly 1,500 or 1,300 °C up to 2,000 °C.
- The process makes metallurgical-grade silicon, not chip-grade silicon. It needs much more purification afterward.

**Claim 1: Chip-grade silicon must be about 99.9999999 percent pure, one foreign atom per billion.**
**Verdict: supported as written, with a caveat.** Nine nines is 99.9999999%, which is one impurity per billion, so the arithmetic holds.
- A US patent says the semiconductor industry needs electronic-grade silicon "having approximately a 99.9999999% purity (9N)." (https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/7727502)
- Wafer World says it must be "at least 99.9999999 percent pure" and calls this "nine-nines" or 9N. (https://www.waferworld.com/post/9-things-you-might-not-have-known-about-silicon-wafers)
- Rapidus says wafers reach 9N purity, and also that semiconductor silicon "generally reaches approximately 99.999999999%" (eleven nines). (https://www.rapidus.inc/en/tech/te0015/)
- Another patent defines electronic-grade silicon as "at least 99.99999 wt %," with a range of 99.9999–99.9999999%. (https://image-ppubs.uspto.gov/dirsearch-public/print/downloadPdf/9238211)
- So 9N is the commonly quoted figure, but the sources differ on the exact requirement. Safer wording: "at least about nine nines pure, with top grades higher."

**Claim 2: A single modern chip can hold over 20 billion transistors.**
**Verdict: supported as written, but don't use the Apple A17 Pro as the example.**
- Wikipedia lists the A17 Pro at 19 billion transistors, which is under 20 billion. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_A17)
- Wikipedia lists the A18 Pro at 20 billion, which is "20 billion," not "over 20." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_A18)
- Wikipedia's Apple M3 page lists the M3 at 25 billion and the M3 Pro at 37 billion. The M3 series spans "25–184 billion." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_M3)
- The claim holds if you cite the M3 or a similar chip. The A17 Pro is a few billion short.

**Claim 3: Spruce Pine, North Carolina supplies most of the world's high-purity quartz used for chipmaking crucibles.**
**Verdict: supported, with the share given as a range.** The sources are secondary and give estimates, not an official figure.
- Wikipedia's High-purity quartz article says high-purity quartz is used to make crucibles in semiconductor manufacturing. It calls the Spruce Pine Mining District in western North Carolina the largest producer of natural high-purity quartz. The mines are operated by Sibelco and The Quartz Corp. (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-purity_quartz)
- Konvoy says Spruce Pine supplies "an estimated 70 to 90 percent" of the world's high-purity quartz used in semiconductor manufacturing. (https://www.konvoy.vc/newsletters/semiconductors-reliance-on-north-carolina)
- Z2Data and Dealroom give the same 70–90% estimate. (https://www.z2data.com/insights/quartz-mine-disruption-in-spruce-pine-nc-threatens-semiconductor-manufacturing/, https://app.dealroom.co/news/note/spruce-pine-the-world-s-most-critical-quartz-choke-point)
- A Substack post gives about 80%. (https://bycig.substack.com/p/the-500-million-mine-holding-up-a)
- Suggested wording: "an estimated 70 to 90 percent of the world's high-purity quartz for semiconductors."
- I found no government source such as USGS in these searches, so the percentage rests on industry commentary.
